children.text: The math. It’s pretty brutal. You have to multiply insanely large matrices in memory. A dense model has to have and multiply across every parameter basically. MoE models work around it, sure, but you still have to hold a lot in memory and density of activated parameters matters. There is not much of a way around it yet. We are potentially getting there, but its not obvious yet.
And what makes decode so memory intensive and seemingly unhackable like the other steps

No commercial service has 200 t/s prefill though. It is 1000s of pps for prefill. It is largely compute bound and very very fast on modern GPUs and model architectures. That is my point. It is an order of magnitude faster than decode, which is largely bound by memory bandwidth and just has a much harder limit. Prefill tends to look like a small slice in typical compute / token generation budgets. I am not saying it isn't important (I have been working hard on my own inference engine for flash next and am intimately familiar). I am saying it does not dominate. Also compaction and reading the whole prompt tends to be one of the few times you really hit peak pps because it is cached and you can just fill your data pipes for a bit. Also Deepseek showed you can make kv cache really cheap. Decode is still decode.

Isn’t input so much cheaper because it’s just less work? Prefill is usually 10-20x as fast as generation.

If you have 200k context, but only 200t/s prefill, then you’ll wait multiple minutes when continuing an average session from yesterday. Or compaction - might take 15 minutes.

It doesn’t. Decode is by far the most dominant and expensive part of agentic tasks and once prefill hits a certain achievable speed decode dominates the time in ant agentic flows with reasoning. There is a reason input is so much cheaper :)
Why does agentic work live and die by prefill speeds?

The really expensive part of inference - the compute and memory traffic required to perform prompt processing and decode - is paid for roughly once per token in a multi-turn session when prompt caching is working properly.

The difference to the provider's costs between:

- Submitting 100 back-to-back requests, each adding 1k tokens to the context

- Submitting 1 100k token context request

Is negligible. Yet the consumer is going to pay a lot more in the former case for all those repeatedly submitted input tokens that you get charged the cached rate for (but which required no additional compute on the provider side).

DeepSeek V4.1 has an insanely optimized KV-cache that takes around 900MB per million tokens, making it feasible to move to disk between requests. Makes sense they're cheap

children.text:
That's a short-term view of a subset of users.

Think about mobile users. If you compare the raw cost for MVNOs vs MNOs, they have basically the same cost. There is no special moat around text messages, voice calls, data. By law, MNOs have to give MVNOs access to resell their network access; it's literally the same network. Yet MVNOs are 2x-6x cheaper than MNOs. How is that possible? Trickery. MNOs hide fees, bundle "features", lock people into exorbitant prices, and increase costs over time. Nobody today sees the price per minute of calls, text, data. If you look really, really closely, you can compare data caps, international vs domestic. But almost nobody does.

Now back to LLMs: Normal users do not pay API cost, they pay subscription cost. They're going to be the vast majority of users. No normal user is going to look at API provider costs. They're going to pick one of a handful of subscription providers. Those subscription providers will hide the real costs behind the scenes, making deals with inference providers, who will in turn hide those prices for competitive advantage. They will raise prices, and it'll be buried in the subscription fees. This has been happening for a decade with mobile subscriptions, and it's already happening now with LLM subscriptions. (There is no price-list for current LLM subscriptions; it's a total mess that's constantly changing)

Enterprise and government are large-scale users, and they'll pay exactly the same way they pay for compute right now (LLM cost is literally compute cost). Some will self-host, some will pay API pricing, some will rent, some will use "team" or "business" subscriptions. This is also all happening right now. AWS is making bank from Bedrock purely because people in their ecosystem would rather spend money through a known vendor with marketplace credits, and that's just one of a hundred different examples.

To put it in simpler terms: AI is just servers. Normal people do not pay for servers, they pay a service provider for services. Businesses pay for servers, but in many different ways, and definitely not the cheapest options.

> Rather than cost to consumers going down over time, it will likely go up. Not because it can't get cheaper/more efficient - but because it increases companies' profit.

As shown in the OpenRouter links you provided, there are over 30 distinct providers of these open-weights models, the majority of them supporting ZDR. They can't raise prices because it's a near-perfect marketplace and if they do, someone will just lower them to compete as long as marginal revenue >= marginal cost. There's no moat or other economic factors (e.g. collusion; hard to do with 30 actors) to allow for price control.

That still isn't the whole story. Compare DS 4.1 Flash [1] to GLM 5.3 Flash [2], and consider the effective price. DS's price is lower than GLM on input tokens, but higher than GLM on output tokens. Output price is an order of magnitude higher than input price. So for output-heavy workloads and long reasoning, DS costs more than GLM.[1] https://openrouter.ai/deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash#pricing [2] https://openrouter.ai/z-ai/glm-5.3-flash#pricing

Yes the official DS provider has a low cache cost, for now (it's just distributed KV). But people are still concerned about ZDR, sovereign AI, getting more model choice in their subscription price, etc. They want more bang for their buck. So when a new model comes out, the bigger impact is really its performance across providers, not the price at a single provider.

And in about 5 years (or less), API prices will stop being a thing. We all used to pay per-minute for phone calls, texts, data. Nobody does anymore. Virtually every mobile provider is now a flat prepaid or contract fee. Carriers improved their technology (going from analog to digital), and it turned out consumers will spend more money on a packaged subscription than on pay-per-use. That's why everything in the world is a subscription now.

Your modern $70 big wireless plan isn't giving you $70 of value. Similarly, your $20 AI subscription that's a great deal right now, will be less valuable in 5 years, when hardware & models are more efficient. You'll still be able to buy a local AI rig, but it will still be very expensive, due to AI models continuing to be large, and NVidia keeping new hardware expensive, as these things together reinforce their dominance and profits, and our reliance on them.

This also follows another pre-existing trend. Why do people keep having to buy a new iPhone or laptop every other year? Because each year companies make software & data less efficient/more bloated, so people need a more powerful machine to run it, which enables them to make even more bloated software. Almost everything people do with a computer today is what they did 15-20 years ago; it's just a higher bit-rate. Despite this, people keep re-buying the same machine, so companies can keep extracting more wealth.

AI works the same way. Rather than cost to consumers going down over time, it will likely go up. Not because it can't get cheaper/more efficient - but because it increases companies' profit. This isn't just a theory, btw; the US economy's growth is now almost entirely reliant on this happening.

children.author: Saline9515
children.text: With the old GPT-3 api in the olden days, you could set the seed and get deterministic outputs! Interesting results could be drawn from it, as for instance if you use the prompts "a blue bird"/"a blue bird in the sky" the blue bird would have the same look in both with similar seeds.

in practice, as actually used, LLMs are nondeterministic.

It is possible, if you control the execution environment sufficiently, and are careful not to use certain kinds of parallelism which can lead to nondeterminism, and you set the seed deterministically and ensure that the prompts are byte identical, you can operate them deterministically.

But no one actually does all of that. Almost everyone uses cloud hosted APIs where the provider could change any number of variables at any time. Everyone wants faster cheaper inference so uses inference engines which may trade off a certain amount of determinism for more speed. Different versions of harnesses and chat templates and benchmark software may introduce small differences in text.

And even though the cloud providers have in the past offered seed and system fingerprints to try to give people a way to control or detect non-determinism (see https://developers.openai.com/cookbook/examples/reproducible...), that has all been deprecated and removed in the newer APIs.

So yeah, while in theory it's possible that if you control the whole stack you can get deterministic results, that's not how anyone is using it, and there is no way for third party benchmarks to ensure deterministic results of hosted models, the latest APIs don't even support it at all.

This whole "well, actually, LLMs are deterministic if you hold them right" is a red herring. In any actual real-world use, they are basically always non-deterministic.

And of course, there are reasons that providers have dropped these attempts at providing deterministic results; because the results are chaotic, perturbed by small changes in input, it's almost never useful to try to make them act deterministic or detect when non-determinism has happend. Instead, it's better to think about them non-deterministically, and look at the distribution of results, rather than just considering a single pass or fail on a single test to be meaningful.

> LLMs are nondeterministic

Being pedantic - LLMs are deterministic software, that is chaotic and typically deployed with a PRNG seed. An LLM ran using the same seed will produce the same output consistently (theoretically - in practice this isn’t always the case because of changing factors wrt the execution environment given how sensitive/chaotic models are).

Because they selectively choose which benchmarks to highlight and which competing models to compare against; they don't always compare against the SOTA or the Pareto frontier of performance/price, a lot of times you'll see them compare against the last generation of competing models, or the like, so that they look better if you don't carefully consider what they're comparing against.

For example, here you see they are comparing against Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol, when Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6 Astra, and GPT-6.1 Sol would be the latest SOTA models from those labs to compare against.

Also because a lab's own benchmarks tend to run about 6.4% better than third party runs of the same benchmark. Source: https://whatmodel.sh/claims This can happen due to a number of factors, and doesn't necessarily indicate anything nefarious. It could just be that they run multiple times while fixing issues that aren't related to the model, and have a selection bias towards stopping when the score is on the higher side. But since you see that sometimes their own scores are lower than the independent runs, some of the variation is explained just by variance in the model solving problems, since LLMs are nondeterministic there can be variation from run to run and you don't see labs always cheating, just potentially a bit of selection bias about when they stop tweaking their benchmark setup and publish the results.

And yes, there are independent third party runs of benchmarks for just this reason. The most popular with broad coverage of a range of benchmarks is https://artificialanalysis.ai/ but there are a number of others as well.

> Announcements are crafted by publicity teams and involve cherry picking a chart that looks compelling.

*crafted by LLMs with a list of PR guidelines in a markdown file

There are hundreds of benchmarks (all noisy), dozens of model families, and dozens of modes and variants within each. Announcements are crafted by publicity teams and involve cherry picking a chart that looks compelling.

As a prospective user, none of of the benchmarks details will matter to you, but the family of models and settings they peg themselves against can give you a hint of where you might want to evaluate them within your own workflows.

As an enthusiast or lay researcher, the more interesting thing is to look at their techniques and any innovations they're exploring in training, inference, etc. Those are usually going to be details tucked below the fold and won't be summarized in a benchmark chart.

As anybody else, why do you even care about this in the first place?

This doesn't just apply to AI. You should know better than to take marketing announcements at face value, nor trust that most "influencers" or "journalists" or "commenter" repeating and discussing those announcements are doing a lot of work as they buzz over what's said.

Don't be a victim to PR spin, but also don't discount potentially interesting work just because it got channeled through a marketing team. Just look for the information you need amidst the noise or move on if there's none there.
